ogDesc: Start with the Andaman Sea and Ranong's hot springs, then drive across the peninsula to collect Chumphon's Gulf beaches and seafood. Real routes, real spots, real prices.
h1:
Ranong–Chumphon: 3 Days, 2 Nights
Across the Peninsula from Andaman to Gulf
intro: Ranong and Chumphon sit on opposite sides of the Kra Peninsula, but they're only about two and a half hours apart by road over the hills. So this trip gives you two seas in one go. You start on the Andaman side in Ranong, soaking at the Raksawarin hot springs in the middle of town, then heading out to Koh Phayam, where the water is clearer and the pace is slower. After that you drive across the peninsula to the Gulf side in Chumphon for Sai Ri Beach, the Krom Luang shrine, and fresh seafood. This 3-day, 2-night plan comes with real routes, real timings, and rough prices you can adjust to suit yourself.

blocks.html: What makes a Ranong–Chumphon trip fun is that it hands you two different worlds within easy reach. Ranong is the Andaman side: heavy rain, green forest, natural hot springs right in town, and islands with clearer water than the Gulf. Chumphon is the Gulf side: a long stretch of coast with sandy beaches, seafood, and robusta coffee. You drive Highway 4 (Phetkasem) over a short hilly stretch and the whole mood changes. This plan front-loads two days in Ranong so you can do the hot springs and Koh Phayam properly, then crosses over on the last day to finish in Chumphon.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: Ranong is famous for being the rainiest province in Thailand — locals joke it's eight months of rain and four of sun. The window for clear seas and calm water, ideal for getting out to Koh Phayam, is November to April, with March and April being the driest and flattest. During the monsoon (May to October) boats are cancelled on some days. If you come then, flip the plan and take Koh Phayam on whichever early day the sky opens up, keeping the hot springs and waterfalls — which you can still visit in the rain — as your backup.

The idea is to start with the sea and hot springs on the west side, then drive across to finish on the Gulf. Day one is a full day out on Koh Phayam, with your first night either in Ranong town or on the island. Day two covers mainland Ranong — soaking at the Raksawarin hot springs, stopping by a waterfall and Wat Ban Ngao — with your second night back in Ranong town. Day three is an early checkout, a drive over the hills to Chumphon for Sai Ri Beach and the Krom Luang shrine, a Pak Nam seafood lunch, then the trip home from Chumphon, which has both a train station and an airport. This works best if you drive yourself, since public transport between the provinces and out to the sights is limited.

items: Day 1 — Full day on Koh Phayam, the Andaman Sea, overnight in Ranong town or on the island
Day 2 — Mainland Ranong, Raksawarin hot springs, waterfall, Wat Ban Ngao, overnight in Ranong town
Day 3 — Drive over the hills to Chumphon, Sai Ri Beach, the Krom Luang shrine, Pak Nam seafood, then head home
Ranong–Chumphon drive — About 120–130 km, roughly 2 to 2.5 hours

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Out to Koh Phayam, a full Andaman day

items.activity: Head to the Ranong pier and catch the boat to Koh Phayam — about 45 min by speedboat, around 2 hours by slow boat
items.note: Check the boat schedule ahead of time; morning runs get crowded on weekends

items.activity: Arrive on Koh Phayam, rent a motorbike on the island, and head for Ao Yai and Ao Khao Kwai
items.note: No cars run on the island — a motorbike is the main way to get around

items.activity: Swim at the white-sand beach and laze under the trees; the water is clearer than on the Gulf side
items.note: Koh Phayam gets called Thailand's Maldives by some

items.activity: Lunch at a beachfront spot on the island — fresh seafood and made-to-order dishes
items.note: Prices on the island run a little higher than on the mainland because of shipping costs — that's normal

items.activity: Ride past the cashew orchards to catch a sunset spot, or take a small boat out to the clear-water spots around the island
items.note: Some operators run half-day boat tours around the island, such as nearby Koh Khang Khao (Bat Island)

items.activity: Catch the boat back to mainland Ranong, or stay a night on the island if you want quiet beaches in the morning
items.note: If you head back, leave time — the evening boats fill up fast on weekends

items.activity: Check into your place in Ranong town, have a seafood dinner in town, and rest up for the mainland day tomorrow
items.note: Staying in town keeps you close to the hot springs and makes the next day easy

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Mainland Ranong: Raksawarin hot springs, a waterfall, and Wat Ban Ngao

items.activity: Breakfast of Ranong dim sum — pork dumplings, steamed buns, bak kut teh — in town
items.note: Dim sum is the local breakfast staple, with a Hokkien-Chinese feel

items.activity: Head into Raksawarin Park to soak your feet in the natural hot springs in the middle of town — the Father, Mother, and Child pools
items.note: The water sits around 65°C, clear with no sulphur smell; the foot-soaking pools are open all day and free

items.activity: Stop by Punyaban Waterfall near town — about a 10-minute walk from the car park to the falls
items.note: The waterfall is near the airport and easy to visit even in light rain

items.activity: Lunch in Ranong town — try Hokkien-style noodles or seafood at a local spot
items.note: Ranong food carries a mix of Hokkien-Chinese and Burmese influences

items.activity: Visit Wat Ban Ngao to see the large tin Buddha image and the fish sanctuary; if you're up for it, climb to the 360° viewpoint
items.note: The climb to the viewpoint is around 343 steps, steep and narrow — take it slow

items.activity: Head up to the Phukhao Ya (Grass Mountain) viewpoint — bare hills that turn green in the rainy season and brown grassland in the dry
items.note: It's a short walk up, with views all around from the top — good for the late-afternoon light

items.activity: Back into Ranong town for a seafood dinner or the evening market, and pick up some cashews and coffee to take home
items.note: Pack your bags ready — tomorrow has the cross-province drive

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Across the peninsula to Chumphon: Sai Ri Beach and Gulf seafood

items.activity: Check out, leave Ranong town, and drive Highway 4 north toward Chumphon
items.note: Fill up the tank before you go — gas stations are spread out over the hilly stretch

items.activity: Stop on the way to grab Tap Lee steamed buns for the road — both sweet and savoury fillings to snack on over the hills
items.note: Bun shops line up around Tap Lee; they're the classic snack on this route

items.activity: Reach Chumphon, take a breather in town, then head toward Sai Ri Beach
items.note: It's about 20 minutes from Chumphon town to Sai Ri Beach

items.activity: Seafood lunch along the Sai Ri road — fresh fish straight from the small-scale Gulf fishermen
items.note: Blue crab, grilled prawns, and grilled squid are fresh and well-priced on this side

items.activity: Pay respects at the Krom Luang Chumphon shrine, and take in the navy ship and the wide Gulf view
items.note: Dress modestly when entering the shrine grounds

items.activity: Stroll along Sai Ri Beach to close out the trip, comparing the Gulf with the Andaman you just came from
items.note: The two seas have totally different moods — fun to have photos of both to compare

items.activity: Head into Chumphon town and travel home from the train station or Chumphon airport, or stay one more night
items.note: Chumphon has both a train and an airport, so it's easier to leave from than Ranong

blocks.title: If it's pouring on your island day
blocks.html: Ranong rains easily, and boats out to the island depend on the swell. If the sky won't clear on day one, swap the mainland day forward instead: soak at the Raksawarin hot springs, walk to Punyaban Waterfall just 10 minutes or so from the airport, or stop by the Por Rang hot mineral springs inside Ngao Waterfall park, which is quieter. Then save Koh Phayam for a day with less swell.

blocks.text: Which hot springs to soak in around Ranong

blocks.html: Ranong is a genuine mineral-water town with several natural hot springs. The easiest and most free option is Raksawarin in the middle of town. It has three pools — the Father, the Mother, and the Child — with water around 65°C and no sulphur in it. If you have time to spare, there are other springs spread around the province to suit your style, from natural soaking pools in the forest to resort onsens you pay extra for.

items.name: Raksawarin Hot Springs
items.blurb: Natural hot springs in the middle of town, three pools, water around 65°C, clear with no sulphur smell. Free foot-soaking all day; if you want to soak your whole body, there's an indoor zone that opens in time slots for a fee in the tens of baht.

items.name: Por Rang Hot Mineral Springs
items.blurb: Mineral springs inside Ngao Waterfall park, about 10 km from town. The setting is more natural and quieter than Raksawarin — good if you want to dodge the crowds.

items.name: Resort onsens
items.blurb: Plenty of resorts in Ranong pipe hot mineral water into the rooms or build private onsen pools. Good if you want to soak in comfort without sharing — you pay extra, but it's private.

blocks.text: Where to eat along the route

blocks.html: This route lets you eat in two styles. The Ranong side carries a mix of Hokkien-Chinese and Burmese influence, with seafood that's fresh and cheap, while Chumphon is Gulf seafood and robusta coffee. The list below is ordered by when you'd likely stop along the trip, not a ranking of which spot beats another. Double-check each place's closing days and opening hours before you go, just to be safe.

items.name: Beachfront spot on Koh Phayam
items.blurb: A beachfront restaurant on the island, eating seafood with your feet in the sand and the Andaman Sea in front of you. Prices run a touch higher than the mainland because of the cost of shipping out to the island, but the setting earns it. This is your day-one lunch.
items.meta: Ao Yai / Ao Khao Kwai, Koh Phayam

items.name: Raan Prung, Ranong
items.blurb: A breakfast spot Ranong locals know well, on Chaloem Phrakiat Road. Dim sum, pork dumplings, steamed buns, stewed-pork-leg rice, pan-fried eggs, and bak kut teh — a day-two opener with a southern-Chinese flavour.
items.meta: Chaloem Phrakiat Rd, Ranong town · opens early

items.name: Ranong Hokkien noodles
items.blurb: Yellow noodles stir-fried Hokkien-style, a rounded southern-Chinese flavour that Ranong does well. A good day-two lunch after the hot springs and the waterfall walk.
items.meta: Ranong town · a stall in the market

items.name: Somboon Phochana, Ranong
items.blurb: A local seafood restaurant in Ranong town with fresh ingredients, including lobster and Andaman-side seafood. Good for a day-one dinner after getting back from the island.
items.meta: Ranong town · opens evening into the night

items.name: Suan Lung Worn Cafe
items.blurb: A white glass-house cafe in the forest beside a stream in Ranong, with coffee and bakery and a cool, shady setting. Good for a breather between mainland stops on day two.
items.meta: Outskirts of Ranong · check opening hours first

items.name: Ranong evening market
items.blurb: Wallet-friendly dinner food — savoury, sweet, and fried — that you can graze on for a while. Good for a night when you want to eat cheap and easy near your place.
items.meta: Ranong town · open evening into the night

items.name: Tap Lee steamed buns
items.blurb: The well-known snack on the way out of Ranong: steamed buns with generous sweet and savoury fillings. Shops line up around Tap Lee — good to grab for the road as you drive over the hills to Chumphon.
items.meta: Tap Lee area, on the Ranong–Chumphon route

items.name: Krua Je Ang, Pak Nam Chumphon
items.blurb: A roadside seafood restaurant on the way to the Krom Luang shrine, with fresh ingredients from the small-scale Gulf fishermen. Plenty of standout dishes — fried fish, sour curry, and spicy salads — making it a good last-day lunch stop.
items.meta: Pak Nam Chumphon · on the way to Sai Ri Beach

items.name: Mae Mai Seafood, Chumphon
items.blurb: A seafood restaurant along the Chumphon–Pak Nam road with a relaxed setting and a full seafood menu — blue crab, prawns, squid. The kind of place locals bring guests to.

items.name: Robusta Station, Chumphon
items.blurb: A cafe on Phetkasem Road in Chumphon using well-selected Chumphon robusta. There are local goods to take home too, from roasted coffee to southern curries. Good for a stop before heading home.
items.meta: Phetkasem Rd, Chumphon · last stop of the trip

blocks.text: Where to base yourself for this plan

blocks.html: This plan stays mostly two nights in Ranong, since day one is the island and day two is the mainland — both on this side. The last day you drive over to Chumphon and head straight home. If you'd rather split a night in Chumphon, you can stretch it to four days. Pick your zone based on where you need to be the next morning, and you'll save a lot of early-morning driving.

items.name: First night, Ranong town
items.blurb: Close to the Koh Phayam pier and the Raksawarin hot springs. Some places have their own mineral onsen pools, good for a soak before bed after getting back from the island, and an easy start to the mainland day.

items.name: On Koh Phayam
items.blurb: If you really want the sea to the full, stay on the island your first night. Wake up to quiet beaches and watch the sunrise before heading back to the mainland. Good if you have time to spare and aren't in a rush.

items.name: Last night, Chumphon town
items.blurb: If you don't want a long drive home in one day, stay a night in Chumphon, near the market and the robusta cafes, then leave from the Chumphon train station or airport the next morning.

blocks.text: Getting around and what to pack

blocks.html: A cross-province trip like this works best by self-drive, since public transport between Ranong and Chumphon and out to the sights is limited. If you're not driving in, you can fly or take a coach into Ranong and rent a car. For Koh Phayam, park at the Ranong pier and take the boat, then rent a motorbike on the island, since no cars run there. The trip home from Chumphon is easier, with both the southern rail line and an airport.

items: Car rental — easiest for a cross-province plan; leave extra time for the curves on the Highway 4 hill stretch
For the island — swimwear, sunscreen, a waterproof phone pouch, and seasickness pills
For the hot springs — clothes you don't mind getting wet, a towel, and easy slip-off sandals
Rain jacket — Ranong rains easily even outside the monsoon; carrying one is reassuring
Cash — local shops, boat tours, and many places on the island take cash first

blocks.text: Want a Ranong-only plan before crossing to Chumphon?
blocks.label: See the Ranong travel guide →

faq.q: Is Ranong far from Chumphon? How many hours to drive?
faq.a: Not far. It's about 120–130 km from Ranong town to Chumphon town, driving Highway 4 (Phetkasem) over a hilly stretch, roughly 2 to 2.5 hours. Fill the tank before crossing the hills since gas stations are spread out, and there are Ranong–Chumphon minivans running on schedule during the day if you're not driving yourself.

faq.q: Is there an entry fee for the Raksawarin hot springs?
faq.a: The outdoor foot-soaking pools are free and open all day. There are three pools — the Father, the Mother, and the Child — with water around 65°C and no sulphur smell. If you want to soak your whole body in the indoor zone, there's a small fee in the tens of baht per person, and that zone opens in time slots, so check the schedule on site.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Ranong–Chumphon?
faq.a: November to April is best, with clear skies and calm seas — especially March and April, when Ranong gets little rain and Koh Phayam is easy to reach. May to October is the monsoon, with boats cancelled on some days; if you come then, focus on the hot springs and waterfalls you can visit in the rain, and take your chances on the island on a low-swell day.

faq.q: Do you have to stay overnight on Koh Phayam?
faq.a: No. If you come early and leave in the evening, you can cover the main beaches in a single day. It's about 45 minutes by speedboat or around 2 hours by slow boat from the Ranong pier. But if you want quiet beaches in the morning and a pretty sunset, staying a night on the island and stretching the plan to four days is worth it.

faq.q: Can you do this plan without your own car?
faq.a: You can, but it takes more planning. Flying or taking a coach into Ranong and renting a car is easiest, since public transport to the sights is limited. For Koh Phayam, park at the Ranong pier and take the boat, then rent a motorbike on the island to get around. There are Ranong–Chumphon minivans during the day for the crossing, and the trip home from Chumphon has both a train and an airport.
